target.title: fix(gateway): bound busy channel health by real run age
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`evaluateChannelHealth` intentionally treats a channel as healthy while a run is in flight, even when the transport already reports `connected: false`. That busy override is meant to be bounded by a 25 minute stale ceiling, but the ceiling is measured from `lastRunActivityAt`, which the run-state heartbeat refreshes every 60 seconds for as long as any run is active.

If a per-message task hangs forever, for example a channel send blocking on a half-open or dead socket with no send timeout after the transport disconnected, `onRunEnd` never fires, the heartbeat keeps ticking, and `lastRunActivityAt` never ages past roughly 60 seconds. The `>= 25min` stuck branch, the only escape from busy-overrides-disconnected, becomes permanently unreachable. The account is then reported healthy forever by the channel health monitor (`if (health.healthy) continue`), the readiness probe (`src/gateway/server/readiness.ts`), and the `openclaw health` CLI (`src/commands/health.ts`). No restart fires and no operator-visible signal appears until the process is restarted. Transport disconnects mid-send with no send timeout are a normal production failure mode.

## Why This Change Was Made

The busy override must be bounded by how long the run has actually been in flight, not by a timestamp the heartbeat keeps fresh. A single hung run must eventually breach the stale ceiling.

Root cause, `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts` busy branch (before):

```ts
const runActivityAge =
  lastRunActivityAt == null
    ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
    : Math.max(0, policy.now - lastRunActivityAt);
if (runActivityAge < BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS) {
  return { healthy: true, reason: "busy" };
}
return { healthy: false, reason: "stuck" };
```

`lastRunActivityAt` is republished as `now()` on every heartbeat tick in `createRunStateMachine`, so `runActivityAge` never grows while a run hangs.

Fix. `createRunStateMachine` now tracks each in-flight run's start time keyed by an opaque run handle returned from `onRunStart` and passed back to `onRunEnd`, and publishes the oldest still-active run's start as `activeRunStartedAt`. When the oldest run ends the reported start advances to the next-oldest, and it clears when no run is active. The health policy busy branch keys the ceiling off the real run age (after):

```ts
const runStartAge =
  activeRunStartedAt == null ? null : Math.max(0, policy.now - activeRunStartedAt);
const runActivityAge =
  lastRunActivityAt == null ? null : Math.max(0, policy.now - lastRunActivityAt);
const busyAge =
  runStartAge == null && runActivityAge == null
    ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
    : Math.max(runStartAge ?? 0, runActivityAge ?? 0);
if (busyAge < BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS) {
  return { healthy: true, reason: "busy" };
}
return { healthy: false, reason: "stuck" };
```

Because the oldest active run's start is fixed while that run is in flight and the heartbeat only advances `lastRunActivityAt`, a run stuck longer than the threshold now reports `stuck`. Because the reported start is the oldest active run and advances as runs complete, a channel churning through many short overlapping runs stays healthy; only a genuinely hung run breaches the ceiling. The `activeRunStartedAt` field flows through the same run-state to snapshot path as `lastRunActivityAt` (`run-state-machine.ts` publish, `account-snapshot-fields.ts` read, `types.core.ts` snapshot type), so all three consumers of `evaluateChannelHealth` (monitor, readiness, CLI) get the corrected verdict.

## Why This Is The Right Boundary

The masking lives in one shared decision function, `evaluateChannelHealth`, consumed by the monitor, readiness probe, and health CLI, so a single change fixes all three surfaces. The heartbeat that defeats the ceiling lives in `createRunStateMachine`, the one owner of run activity status, so the run-age fact is surfaced where it is produced rather than re-derived per caller. `createChannelRunQueue` shares one run-state machine across all queue keys and `KeyedAsyncQueue` runs unrelated keys concurrently, so `activeRuns` routinely exceeds 1; tracking the oldest active run rather than a busy-streak start keeps a continuously busy account healthy while still catching a single hung run. Legitimate busy behavior is preserved: short, active, and overlapping runs stay healthy, and snapshots without a start time fall back to the previous `lastRunActivityAt` behavior. `onRunEnd` now takes the run handle returned by `onRunStart`; the only in-repo caller, `createChannelRunQueue`, is migrated in this same commit, and typed plugin consumers get a compile error rather than silent breakage. Restoring a no-argument `onRunEnd` overload was deliberately avoided because it would reintroduce the counter-decrement accounting this change removes and split run tracking across two paths. The 25 minute ceiling is the pre-existing `BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS` constant; this change only makes it reachable, so a single run in flight past it is now treated as stuck by design. This is distinct from PR #96198, which fixes the same class of heartbeat-hides-stuck bug in the agent diagnostic stuck-session detector (`src/agents/*`, `src/logging/diagnostic-run-activity.ts`), a different subsystem that does not touch channel health.

## User Impact

Channels whose per-message task hangs after a transport disconnect are now detected as stuck once the run exceeds the 25 minute ceiling, so the health monitor restarts them and the outage becomes visible to readiness and the `openclaw health` CLI instead of being silently masked as healthy until a manual process restart.

## Evidence

- New regression test in `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.test.ts`: a disconnected channel with a run in flight longer than the threshold and a fresh heartbeat now evaluates to `{ healthy: false, reason: "stuck" }`. Fails on pristine `main` (returns `busy`), passes with this patch. A companion case keeps a short-lived run `busy`.
- New tests in `src/channels/run-state-machine.test.ts`: across 26 minutes of heartbeat ticks `activeRunStartedAt` stays fixed at the run start while `lastRunActivityAt` advances; and when an older run ends while a newer run is still active the reported start advances to the next-oldest run, so overlapping short runs do not accumulate false age.
- Verification commands (from a deps-enabled checkout):
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/channel-health-policy.test.ts src/channels/run-state-machine.test.ts` passes on this patch.
  - Same test files against pristine `origin/main` source fail on the new stuck assertion.
  - `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs`, `oxfmt --check`, and `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs` (core and core-test) all clean on the changed files.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: a disconnected channel whose per-message run hangs forever is reported healthy forever, because the run-state heartbeat keeps refreshing the activity timestamp that the 25 minute busy ceiling is measured against, so the health monitor never restarts it.
Real environment tested: drove the real periodic health monitor loop from `startChannelHealthMonitor` (`src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.ts`) over the real `evaluateChannelHealth` (`src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts`) fed by a live `createRunStateMachine` (`src/channels/run-state-machine.ts`) with its real `setInterval` heartbeat, on real wall-clock (`Date.now`), on pristine main 091584b1972e86e782860a784607b04448e9b650 and on PR head 21284cf49a131fd39311ed182097a60ff699c3e5. Only the channel transport was stubbed, at the narrowest seam (the `ChannelManager` the monitor calls), so the monitor's real restart recovery path stays observable. Executed on a remote Crabbox AWS lease (c7a.xlarge, eu-west-1, lease cbx_452e9479c6de), not on the author machine. The 25 minute busy ceiling and the 60 second heartbeat were both scaled down 300x (to 5 seconds and 200 milliseconds) so a genuinely hung run breaches the ceiling in seconds of real elapsed time rather than 26 minutes; nothing else was altered and both runs used identical scaling.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: a run begins via the real run-state machine and then hangs (its end callback never fires); the real monitor evaluates the live snapshot every 250 milliseconds while the transport stays connected:false; the harness prints the live snapshot ages and health verdict once per second and the monitor's real restart actions as they occur.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine main 091584b, run hung well past the scaled ceiling)
[health-monitor] started (interval: 0s, startup-grace: 0s, channel-connect-grace: 3600s)
t=1.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=n/a -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=5.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=n/a -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=7.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=n/a -> healthy=true reason=busy
SUMMARY monitorRestarts=0 finalVerdict=busy
# AFTER (PR head 21284cf, identical inputs, identical 300x scaling)
[health-monitor] started (interval: 0s, startup-grace: 0s, channel-connect-grace: 3600s)
t=1.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=1.0s -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=4.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=4.0s -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=5.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=5.0s -> healthy=false reason=stuck
[health-monitor] [telegram:acct-1] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stuck)
  RECOVERY stopChannel(telegram:acct-1)
  RECOVERY startChannel(telegram:acct-1) -> monitor restart #1
t=7.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=7.0s -> healthy=false reason=stuck
SUMMARY monitorRestarts=5 finalVerdict=stuck
```
Observed result after fix: on identical live input, the heartbeat pins lastRunActivityAt age at 0.2s in both runs, so BEFORE the channel stays healthy and busy for the whole hang and the monitor never restarts it (monitorRestarts=0); AFTER, the fixed activeRunStartedAt age grows until it breaches the ceiling, the verdict flips to unhealthy and stuck, and the real health monitor completes its restart recovery path (stopChannel then startChannel) five times over the window. The one value that moves from wrong to right is the health verdict for a hung disconnected channel, and with it the monitor's restart action.
What was not tested: no live provider socket was hung end to end; the hang was a real never-resolving run under the real heartbeat, and the transport was a stub at the ChannelManager seam. The busy ceiling and heartbeat were scaled 300x on real wall-clock so the breach happens in seconds; the unscaled 25 minute breach was not waited out. Full build not run; the change is not on a lazy or packaging boundary.

target.title: fix(google-meet): force English UI when reusing existing Chrome tabs
target.body:
Closes #103385

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `openclaw googlemeet join --mode transcribe` (and `googlemeet.create`) with the Chrome transport would silently fail when an existing Meet tab was rendered in a non-English UI. The plugin's browser automation matches English aria-labels and page text ("Join now", "Turn off microphone", etc.), so a reused tab opened in Japanese or another locale would never reach `inCall: true`, enable captions, or return a meeting URL, with no error pointing at the UI language.

## Why This Change Was Made

The code already forced `?hl=en` when opening a **new** tab, but the reuse path only focused the existing tab. Now, after focusing a reused tab in both the join (`chrome.ts`) and create (`chrome-create.ts`) flows, the plugin navigates the tab to the English variant of its URL before running any DOM-matching automation. If the tab is already using English UI, the URL is unchanged and no navigation is issued.

## User Impact

Users with Google accounts or browser profiles that default Meet to a non-English language can now rely on `googlemeet join`/`create` with the Chrome transport without manually appending `?hl=en` to the URL. Join/status behavior becomes language-independent for reused tabs.

## Evidence

- Focused tests:
  - `pnpm test extensions/google-meet/index.test.ts -- --run` → 116 passed
  - `pnpm test extensions/google-meet/index.create.test.ts -- --run` → 10 passed
  - `pnpm test extensions/google-meet/src/transports/chrome-browser-proxy.test.ts -- --run` → 4 passed

target.title: fix(daemon): self-heal JSON-quoted values in generated service env files (#103804)
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #103804.

The generated gateway service env file could carry entries like `export AWS_REGION='"us-east-1"'` — the value itself wrapped in JSON double quotes inside the correct shell single quotes. Sourcing that file makes the env var the literal string `"us-east-1"`, which the AWS SDK rejects when building the Bedrock endpoint (`Region not accepted: region=""us-east-1"" is not a valid hostname component`).

### Root cause

The writer (`shellSingleQuote`, `src/daemon/launchd.ts`) and every value-loading path (dotenv parsers, SecretRef resolution, auth-profile/config collectors) pass plain strings — none introduces the quotes. What makes the corruption **permanent** is the round-trip reader: `parseGeneratedEnvValue` (`src/daemon/launchd-plist.ts`) strips only the outer shell single quotes when re-reading the previously generated file on re-stage, preserving the inner JSON pair verbatim. The existing-file preservation feed (`collectPreservedExistingServiceEnvVars` / managed-key re-add in `service-env-render-policy.ts`) then copies the still-quoted value into the new plan and the writer re-wraps it — so every `openclaw doctor --fix` regenerates the same broken value and it never self-heals (exactly the reporter's experience: manual edits persist only until the next regeneration).

### Change

`parseGeneratedEnvValue` now strips one redundant enclosing double-quote pair after shell unquoting. The next re-stage converges: `'"us-east-1"'` → `us-east-1` → re-emitted as `'us-east-1'`. Values with interior quotes (`'has "quotes" inside'`) are untouched — only a full wrapping pair is treated as corruption.

## Verification

- New regression `src/daemon/launchd-plist.env-values.test.ts` (confirmed failing without the fix): a real temp plist + generated env file with the corrupted `AWS_REGION` entry heals to `us-east-1`, while a plain value and an interior-quotes value round-trip unchanged.
- `pnpm test src/daemon` — 2 shards passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, oxfmt, oxlint — clean.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: JSON-quoted values in `~/.openclaw/service-env/<label>.env` break AWS region/credentials and survive every `doctor --fix` regeneration.
Real environment tested: the real `readLaunchAgentProgramArgumentsFromFile` reader against a real on-disk plist + generated env file reproducing the issue's exact corrupted entry.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `pnpm test src/daemon/launchd-plist.env-values.test.ts` and `pnpm test src/daemon`.
Evidence after fix: without the patch the new test fails (`AWS_REGION` reads back as `"us-east-1"` with embedded quotes); with it, the value heals to `us-east-1` and non-corrupted values are byte-identical.
Observed result after fix: the re-stage pipeline converges to clean values; manual file edits are no longer required.
What was not tested: a live launchd install/uninstall cycle on a corrupted host; the healed value flows through the same preservation feed the live doctor --fix path uses. How the JSON pair first entered the environment on the reporter's host remains external to this repo (the value arrived already-quoted); this fix guarantees OpenClaw converges instead of locking it in.

target.title: fix(discord): retry reply session init conflicts to prevent silent message loss
target.body:
Closes #102381

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord inbound messages could be silently dropped when a reply session initialization conflict (`reply session initialization conflicted for <sessionKey>`) raced with another turn finishing or another event initializing the same session. Telegram, Signal, and Slack already retry this transient condition; Discord did not, so the user saw no reply and the message was lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added bounded exponential backoff retry inside `processDiscordMessageInner` (`extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.ts`) to match the existing Telegram callback-submit pattern and Slack/Signal retry semantics. The retry only applies to the specific reply-session-init-conflict error string; all other errors fail fast on the first attempt. If the run is aborted while retrying, the loop stops cleanly and returns without throwing.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:** the retry boundary was narrowed so context/history preparation runs exactly once and only the dispatch/session-init attempt is retried. This prevents a Discord room event from being recorded twice when a conflict happens.

## User Impact

Discord users are far less likely to see a missing reply after sending a message that races with a session teardown or concurrent turn. Operators no longer need to ask the user to re-send; the retry covers the brief window where the session store CAS conflict occurs.

## Evidence

- Added a focused regression test suite in `extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts`:
  - retries with exponential backoff until dispatch succeeds (250 ms, 1000 ms, 2500 ms)
  - throws the last error after exhausting retries
  - does not retry unrelated dispatch errors
  - stops retrying when the abort signal fires
  - **records room event history exactly once across conflict retries** (new regression test for the narrowed boundary)
- Full local focused run:
  - `npx vitest run extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-discord.config.ts` → 120 passed
  - `npx vitest run extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.queue.test.ts --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-discord.config.ts` → 22 passed

target.title: fix: severe per-message slowdown when commands.ownerAllowFrom has thousands of entries
target.body:
Closes #50289

## What Problem This Solves

Gateways with large `commands.ownerAllowFrom` lists can spend 15–27 seconds processing each message and emit `lane wait exceeded` warnings. The reporter has 9,282 entries. Command authorization repeatedly trimmed, parsed, channel-filtered, and plugin-formatted the complete list, then used linear array membership checks. That work ran for every inbound message and scaled with the configured list size.

The same behavior is present in the current release and on `main`. PR #103523 improves membership lookup but still constructs the prepared data on every message, so it does not remove the dominant repeated list transformation.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change prepares each configured allow-from array once and carries those facts through the existing command-authorization owner boundary:

- parsed entries and channel filtering;
- plugin-formatted owner and command lists;
- wildcard state; and
- membership `Set`s.

The cache is deliberately scoped by the raw array, `OpenClawConfig` identity, actual plugin implementation identity, provider, account, and owner/command formatting mode. A config reload or plugin-registry replacement therefore cannot reuse stale formatted values. Per-message `ctx.OwnerAllowFrom` overrides retain their existing precedence.

This is the best-fit fix because it removes repeated request-time discovery at the authorization boundary instead of adding another per-message cache or only replacing `.includes`. The shipped mutable `CommandAuthorization.ownerList` SDK shape is preserved with a defensive copy at the public boundary, so callers cannot mutate cached authorization state. That compatibility copy and sender-candidate normalization still run per call; the claim is therefore that the expensive configured-list transformation is reused, not that every operation is strictly O(1).

## User Impact

With a 10,000-entry `ownerAllowFrom`, the production-entry-point harness improved from **17.4 ms/message to 0.009 ms/message** (about 1,900×) while preserving owner, channel-prefix, wildcard, override, and command-allowlist behavior. Small configurations retain the same authorization semantics.

The change is internal to command authorization. It adds no config, migration, protocol, or Plugin SDK surface.

## Evidence

The real-behavior harness calls `resolveCommandAuthorization` with 10,000 mixed channel-prefixed, numeric, and whitespace-padded entries, plus a Discord-shaped plugin formatter.

**Before (`main`):**

```text
[PASS] listed sender is owner
[PASS] unlisted sender is not owner
[PASS] telegram-prefixed entry does not authorize a discord sender
timing: 200 messages, 10000 entries -> 3482 ms total, 17.408 ms/message
[FAIL] authorization stays under 1 ms/message
```

**After (this branch):**

```text
[PASS] listed sender is owner
[PASS] unlisted sender is not owner
[PASS] telegram-prefixed entry does not authorize a discord sender
timing: 200 messages, 10000 entries -> 2 ms total, 0.009 ms/message
[PASS] authorization stays under 1 ms/message
```

`src/auto-reply/command-auth.prepared.test.ts` adds 14 regression tests covering:

- channel-prefixed, numeric, whitespace-padded, cross-channel, and unlisted entries;
- compile-once behavior with a 5,000-entry list;
- provider and account-sensitive formatting;
- shared-array isolation across config identities;
- shared config/array isolation across plugin-registry replacements with the same plugin ID;
- mutation isolation for the SDK-facing `ownerList`;
- `ctx.OwnerAllowFrom` precedence; and
- provider-specific and global `commands.allowFrom` behavior.

Existing focused authorization, Plugin SDK, command-control, stop-target, and subagent-routing suites remain in the CI selection. Repository formatting and `git diff --check` pass. Two independent Codex autoreviews (hardening diff and full PR branch) reported no actionable findings.

[Secretless fork-PR CI run 29120968934](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29120968934) on exact head `9bb38e94dfd` passed production types, test types, every Node test shard, build artifacts, both QA smoke profiles, channel/plugin contracts, dependency guards, and security-fast. Its only failures are current-`main` baselines outside this diff: lint errors in `queue.drain-restart.test.ts` and `server.chat.gateway-server-chat.test.ts`, plus an ACP/agents Madge cycle. The immediately preceding [`main` run 29119824112](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29119824112) failed the same two jobs.

Known proof gap: the contributor-safe AWS Crabbox broker rejected this non-member account before allocating a lease, so no credential-hydrated Testbox was used. The pushed head was instead validated by the repository's secretless fork-PR CI above. A live 9k-user channel deployment was not available; the benchmark uses the production authorization entry point with the bundled Discord formatter's normalization shape. Config-file parsing reported in #50289 is a separate load-time surface and remains out of scope.

---

This PR is AI-assisted (Claude Opus and Codex, human-operated). The final branch was independently reviewed after the cache-lifecycle and SDK-mutation regressions were added.

target.title: fix: deleting a session leaves its trajectory artifacts orphaned on disk
target.body:
Closes #89200

> This PR is AI-assisted: the analysis, patch, and tests were written with an AI coding agent. A human operator reviewed the change and validated it against a live deployment's session store.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where deleting a session (dashboard delete or the `sessions.delete` RPC) leaves its trajectory artifacts orphaned on disk forever. The delete lifecycle archives the transcript but never touches the paired `.trajectory.jsonl` / `.trajectory-path.json` files, and the age-based maintenance path only cleans trajectories for entries it removes itself, so orphans accumulate until the blunt disk-budget sweep (which can also evict live sessions) happens to reclaim them.

## Why This Change Was Made

`deleteSessionEntryLifecycle` now removes the deleted session's trajectory artifacts inside the same exclusive store write, reusing the existing `removeRemovedSessionTrajectoryArtifacts` maintenance helper with the same safeguards as the age-prune path: a referenced-session guard (artifacts are kept while any other store entry still references the session id) and `restrictToStoreDir`. The cleanup is gated on `archiveTranscript`, so a `deleteTranscript: false` delete keeps the trajectory pair together with the preserved transcript.

## User Impact

Deleting a session from the dashboard or via RPC no longer leaks trajectory files into the sessions directory. No configuration change; deletes that keep the transcript keep the trajectory files too, and sessions still referenced by another store entry are untouched.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.runtime-config.config.ts src/config/sessions/store.session-lifecycle-mutation.test.ts src/config/sessions/artifacts.test.ts src/config/sessions/store.pruning.test.ts` passes 40/40, including 2 new tests: trajectory runtime + pointer removed on delete, and kept while another entry still references the same session id.
- Red/green check: with the source change stashed, exactly the new removal test fails (3/4) and restoring the change returns all green.
- Live motivation: on a long-running multi-agent gateway, dashboard session deletes left dozens of orphaned trajectory pairs that no maintenance path ever reclaimed (documented in #89200).
- Full `pnpm build` / `pnpm check` deferred to CI (memory-constrained local host).

target.title: Apply consented grouped Claw updates
target.body:
## Summary

- Extends `claws update <claw-or-agent> --from <source> --yes` behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1` to apply every grouped owner in `openclaw.clawUpdateResult.v1`.
- Rebuilds and compares the read-only plan immediately before mutation, then advances root package/version/integrity provenance only after all owner executors succeed.
- Applies managed workspace file add/change/remove through fs-safe rooted I/O with source digest checks, destination compare-and-swap checks, ownership updates, and guarded rollback.
- Applies MCP add/change/remove through the validated config writer with create-only or expected-value CAS, including remote `sse` / `streamable-http` declarations and credential-free `auth: "oauth"`.
- Applies cron add/change/remove through gateway-owned APIs. Changes must converge on the stable Claw declaration key and existing scheduler id.
- Applies exact ClawHub skill/plugin package versions and updates package references. Removing a reference never implies shared uninstall; conflicting shared plugin version pins fail closed.
- Rolls completed owners back in reverse order when a later owner or root provenance fails. Thrown config/gateway writes and package installs without artifact rollback report `update_partial` instead of claiming atomicity.
- Keeps `--dry-run` read-only and requires explicit `--yes` consent.

This is the final implementation stage in the RFC series: it consumes the preceding read-only plan and adds explicit consent, owner-specific concurrency checks, compensation, and honest partial-state reporting.

Stack references:
- RFC: openclaw/rfcs#27
- Base PR: openclaw/openclaw#102959
- Control UI plugin management alignment: openclaw/openclaw#103176

## Ownership and Control UI alignment

Package references remain per-Claw provenance over shared skill/plugin artifacts. Update-time package removal releases only this Claw's reference. A plugin pinned to a different version by another Claw is not replaced. This keeps CLI lifecycle behavior aligned with the shared uninstall/reference-warning model used by the Control UI rather than creating a second plugin ownership system.

Portable MCP declarations continue to use the validated config surface. They are separate from the Control UI's curated connector shelf and do not persist headers, tokens, or completed OAuth state.

## Real behavior proof

Environment: WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 with isolated config and state.

An installed `@acme/update-proof@1.1.0` agent was previewed and updated to `1.2.0`:

```bash
openclaw claws update update-proof --from ./target-grouped --dry-run --json
openclaw claws update update-proof --from ./target-grouped --yes --json
openclaw claws status update-proof --json
```

The target changed the agent, added `SOUL.md` and `NOTES.md`, and added a remote `streamable-http` OAuth MCP server.

Observed:
- preview reported four unblocked grouped actions;
- apply returned `openclaw.clawUpdateResult.v1` with `status: "complete"`;
- both workspace files matched their target digests;
- the MCP ownership record was `complete` and live state was `present`;
- status reported version `1.2.0`, zero partial records, zero drift, and zero unresolved MCP references;
- the original `addedAtMs` was preserved while `updatedAtMs` advanced.

Cron convergence and exact package installer behavior are covered with injected gateway/installer tests to avoid mutating a developer gateway or shared plugin installation during local proof.

## Validation

- 133 Claw, CLI, lifecycle, config, executor, rollback, and end-to-end tests across 19 files
- non-incremental core TypeScript check: `tsgo -p tsconfig.json --noEmit --incremental false`
- real isolated grouped preview -> consented apply -> status round trip

target.title: fix: skip setup-only channel plugins in outbound resolution and drain pending deliveries on qqbot reconnect
target.body:
## Summary

When the qqbot WebSocket reconnects after a session timeout (close code `4009`), `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()` returns a setup-only plugin stub that lacks any send capability. This causes the `"Outbound not configured for channel: qqbot"` error, and all messages queued during the disconnection window are permanently lost.

## Root Cause

`resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()` resolves the first matching plugin entry for a channel id without verifying that the entry actually has send capability (`outbound.sendText`, `message.send.text`, etc.). During qqbot WebSocket reconnection, a setup-only plugin entry (registered for configuration/pairing but not for message delivery) shadows the real sending plugin, causing the resolution to short-circuit with a non-functional stub.

Regression introduced in 2026.5.28 (commit `e932160`).

## Fix

### 1. Split outbound channel resolution into shared and delivery paths (`channel-resolution.ts`)

Add a `channelPluginCanSend()` predicate that checks for any of the 10 known send methods across both the legacy `outbound` adapter and the newer `message.send` adapter:

- `outbound.sendText / sendMedia / sendPayload / sendPoll / sendFormattedText / sendFormattedMedia`
- `message.send.text / media / payload / poll`

Instead of gating the shared `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()` resolver (which would break action-only channel plugins that have `actions.handleAction` but no send capability), a new **`resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()`** resolver applies the send-capability guard exclusively for message delivery paths.

- **`resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()`**: Shared resolver — returns any matching plugin regardless of send capability, preserving resolution for action dispatch, target resolution, and other non-send callers.
- **`resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()`**: Delivery resolver — skips setup-only entries and only returns plugins that can actually send messages.
- **`resolveOutboundChannelMessageAdapter()`**: Updated to use the delivery resolver.
- **`message.ts`**: `sendMessage`/`sendPoll` updated to use the delivery resolver.

### 2. Align the direct delivery path with the operation-aware resolver (`deliver.ts`)

The preflight resolver was operation-aware, but the actual direct delivery handler reloaded the adapter capability-blind: `createChannelHandler` → `loadBootstrappedOutboundAdapter` → `loadChannelOutboundAdapter` resolved the first registry entry for the channel id (`createChannelRegistryLoader((entry) => entry.plugin.outbound)`) without checking send capability. A setup-only shell with a defined-but-non-send `outbound` (`{ deliveryMode: "direct" }`, no `sendText`) pinned ahead of the runtime sender therefore still shadowed the real adapter on the direct send path, throwing `"Outbound not configured for channel: qqbot"` even after preflight had selected a valid plugin. This also affected the reconnect drain path, which has no preflight.

`loadBootstrappedOutboundAdapter` now resolves through the same `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()` resolver as preflight (with `allowBootstrap`, operation `text`), so preflight and the actual direct delivery handler share one send-capability-aware resolution path. The previous manual bootstrap-and-retry is removed because the resolver's `allowBootstrap` performs the equivalent lazy materialize-then-retry. The generic registry loader and the CLI/SDK surfaces are left untouched.

### 3. Drain pending deliveries on qqbot reconnect (`extensions/qqbot/src/channel.ts`)

The `onReady` and `onResumed` gateway callbacks now call `drainPendingDeliveries()` from the plugin SDK delivery queue runtime, recovering messages that were queued while the WebSocket was disconnected. The drain is:

- Filtered by channel (`qqbot`) and account id, with a fallback for default-account entries where `accountId` may be `undefined`
- Deduplicated via `drainKey` to prevent concurrent drains
- Wrapped in try/catch so drain failures do not break the reconnection flow

### 4. Route the gateway poll handler through the operation-aware resolver (`src/gateway/server-methods/send.ts`)

The gateway `poll` handler still resolved its outbound plugin via the operation-blind `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()`, while `sendPoll` (`message.ts`) and the direct text delivery path (`deliver.ts`) already routed through the operation-aware `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()`. This left the gateway poll endpoint as the last surface where a setup-only / text-only first-match plugin could shadow a poll-capable runtime fallback and force a spurious `"unsupported poll channel"`, even though the new resolver test proves the poll-capable fallback should win.

The poll handler now resolves through `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery({ operation: "poll", allowBootstrap: true })`, mirroring the text delivery path. The `durationSeconds` / `isAnonymous` capability checks below the resolution now read from the same poll-capable plugin that serves `sendPoll`, so the capability gate and the actual send no longer disagree. The two non-poll resolver call sites in the same file (the `send` and `action` surfaces) are intentionally left on the shared resolver, since action-only plugins must still resolve without send capability.

## Tests

- `channel-resolution.test.ts`: setup-only plugin returns from shared resolver, action-only plugin resolves from shared but not delivery resolver, delivery resolver skips setup-only and returns sending fallback, legacy outbound adapter, poll-only outbound
- `deliver.test.ts`: new unmocked regression driving the real `deliverOutboundPayloads` → `createChannelHandler` → `loadBootstrappedOutboundAdapter` path with a pinned setup-only shell that exposes a defined non-send `outbound` plus an active send-capable fallback, asserting the send-capable adapter actually delivers (fails before the Fix 2 alignment with `"Outbound not configured"`, passes after)
- `channel.test.ts`: onReady drain, onResumed drain

Fixes #88955.


## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: After a QQ Bot WebSocket disconnect (session takeover / close code 4009), `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()` returned a setup-only plugin stub instead of the runtime entry, causing `"Outbound not configured for channel: qqbot"` and dropping all pending deliveries.

- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw `2026.6.2` (commit `b90683e`, branch `fix/qqbot-reconnect-outbound-88955`), macOS arm64, Node.js v24.10.0. QQ Bot plugin `@openclaw/qqbot@2026.5.31-beta.4` with live QQ Bot credentials (appId `<redacted>`).

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

- **Observed result after fix**: The delivery resolver correctly skipped the setup-only plugin entry (which has no `sendText`/`sendMedia` methods) and resolved the runtime entry with full send capability. Zero occurrences of the `"Outbound not configured for channel: qqbot"` error across 18 reconnect cycles over a 4+ hour observation window. - **Direct delivery path alignment (follow-up)**: A reviewer noted that the preflight fix did not cover the actual direct delivery handler construction, which reloaded the adapter capability-blind and could still let a pinned setup-only shell shadow the runtime sender. `loadBootstrappedOutboundAdapter` now routes through the same `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()` resolver as preflight. Verified locally on the fix branch (macOS arm64, Node.js v24.10.0): the new unmocked `deliver.test.ts` regression fails before the alignment (`Error: Outbound not configured for channel: matrix` thrown from `createChannelHandler`) and passes after; full focused suite green (`channel-resolution`, `message`, `message.channels`, `deliver`, qqbot `channel` — 169 tests passing), `pnpm tsgo:prod` and `pnpm tsgo:test` clean, `pnpm build` clean, `git diff --check` clean, lint clean.

  **How the delivery queue works** (`deliver.ts:1254-1280`): Every outbound delivery is write-ahead enqueued via `enqueueDelivery()` before any send attempt. On success, `ackDelivery()` removes the entry (`deliver.ts:1367`). On throw, `failDelivery()` bumps `retryCount` and **leaves it pending** (`delivery-queue-storage.ts:137-144`).

  **What created the pending entries in #88955**: The `"Outbound not configured for channel: qqbot"` throw fired from `createChannelHandler` (`deliver.ts:223-231`) when `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery` returned a setup-only plugin with no send methods.   **Why transient QQ API failures also do not create pending entries**: The qqbot engine **swallows** HTTP/network errors into returned `{error}` result objects instead of throwing (`outbound.ts:301-304, 313-318`). The `bypassBackoff` predicate explicitly matches this exact error string (`/outbound not configured/i`), ensuring these entries skip retry backoff and are retried on the first reconnect event. If the retry still fails (e.g., the plugin is genuinely misconfigured), `isPermanentDeliveryError` (`delivery-queue-recovery.ts:79`) moves the entry to `failed/` — no infinite retry loop. `MAX_RETRIES` is also enforced before the bypass branch (`delivery-queue-recovery.ts:544`). The entry was successfully delivered (HTTP 200) and acked (removed from queue).

A naturally-occurring live drain on the `onReady` path cannot be reliably reproduced because the fix removes the deterministic failure that created those entries, and startup recovery pre-empts the reconnect drain for entries present at boot. target.title: fix(gateway): reload plugin code across in-process restarts (#103571)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

An in-process gateway restart (SIGUSR1 / `gateway restart --safe` under `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1`) re-runs each plugin's `register()` and logs `<plugin> registered` — but serves the module graph cached from the original process start. Cached plugin registries survive the restart boundary (`pluginLoaderCacheState`), and native-required JS entrypoints stay in Node's shared `require.cache`, so updated **workspace plugin code** on disk (e.g. a newly registered tool) never takes effect until a full process restart. Config changes *do* reload because the restart iteration hook already calls `clearRuntimeConfigSnapshot()` — plugin caches were the missing symmetric clear. Fixes #103571.

## Why This Change Was Made

Restart is the repo's documented **explicit reload boundary** for process-stable plugin state ("Plugin metadata changes require restart or explicit plugin owner reload/install/doctor flow" — `src/plugins/AGENTS.md`). Add `clearPluginCachesForInProcessRestart()` in the plugins loader (drops cached registries + activated runtime state, manifest read caches, and purges previously imported plugin entrypoints from `require.cache`), exported through the gateway lifecycle runtime facade and called from the run-loop restart iteration hook next to the config snapshot clear, **before** the next startup. No steady-state freshness polling is introduced — the clear runs only at the explicit restart boundary. No new options or public API surface.

## User Impact

Operators running in-process restarts (the docs-recommended systemd setup on small hosts) get what the `registered` log already implies: an updated workspace plugin (new tool, changed behavior) is live after `openclaw gateway restart --safe`, instead of silently stale until a full process restart.

## Evidence

Two tests, both discriminating:
- `run-loop.test.ts` — the restart-iteration hook must call the plugin cache clear alongside the existing lane/config resets. **Fails on main** (`clearPluginCachesForInProcessRestart` never called: `1 failed | 40 passed`), passes with this PR (41/41).
- `loader.restart-reload.test.ts` (new) — real temp workspace plugin registering `probe_tool_v1` → source+manifest edited on disk to `probe_tool_v2` → reload **without** the clear still serves v1 (reproduces the reported staleness) → reload **after** `clearPluginCachesForInProcessRestart()` loads `probe_tool_v2` from disk.

`tsgo:core` 0 errors; `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean.

target.title: [Bug]: Signal quoted replies can lose quoted context in BodyForAgent
target.body:
## Bug type
Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Beta release blocker
No

## Summary
Signal quoted-reply context can be extracted into `ReplyToBody` / related metadata while `BodyForAgent` remains only the new ambiguous message body, so agent-facing paths that rely on `BodyForAgent` can miss the quoted target.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Configure the Signal channel and receive an inbound Signal message.
2. From Signal, quote/reply to that message with an ambiguous body such as `Did this get done?`.
3. Inspect the inbound context handed to the agent/prompt-building path.

## Expected behavior
The agent-facing input reliably includes the quoted target, either as a clear quoted block in `BodyForAgent` or through another prompt-builder-guaranteed surface that survives retries/session handoff. A useful rendered shape is:

```text
Quoted Signal reply context from sender:
> original quoted message

Did this get done?
```

Session retries, queued followups, and handoff paths should preserve the quote-enhanced agent-facing context. Plain non-quoted Signal messages should remain unchanged, and normalization should not duplicate the quote block.

## Actual behavior
`ReplyToBody` / quote metadata can exist, but `BodyForAgent` can be just the ambiguous new body, for example `Did this get done?`. Paths that consume the current message body directly may therefore omit the quoted target even though the adapter extracted it elsewhere.

## OpenClaw version
Current `main` before the proposed fix, and observed against a recent npm-installed OpenClaw runtime with the Signal adapter. Exact released build: NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

## Operating system
Linux/macOS deployments are affected by the Signal adapter shape; exact OS for a minimal upstream repro: NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

## Install method
npm global and source checkout investigation

## Model
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

## Provider / routing chain
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

## Additional provider/model setup details
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

## Logs
```shell
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO
```

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence
Local source investigation shows the Signal adapter computes visible quote context and stores it on reply metadata fields, while the agent-facing body can remain the new message body. A local post-update workaround inlined the quote into the agent body with the quoted-block shape shown above.

## Impact and severity
Affected: Signal users sending quoted replies to an OpenClaw agent.
Severity: Medium to high, because short replies such as `Did this get done?` or `what about this?` can become unintelligible to the model.
Frequency: Whenever a quoted Signal reply depends on the quoted target and the consuming path sees only `BodyForAgent`.
Consequence: The agent may answer the wrong item or ignore the intended quoted context.

## Additional information
Related but non-duplicate: #98234 covers Signal reply-session initialization conflict retry/drop behavior. This issue is specifically about preserving quoted Signal context in the agent-facing body/text. Older Signal quote issues/PRs cover native quote support or queued structured metadata, but this report is the narrower `BodyForAgent` agent-facing context gap.

target.title: fix(reply): add per-hook timeout with timer cleanup in combineBeforeDeliverHooks (#103684)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a channel `beforeDeliver` hook never resolves or rejects, `waitForIdle()`
blocks forever. The `sendChain` is permanently stuck, subsequent replies are
never delivered, and the lane stays blocked. Reported on WhatsApp with
`2026.6.11` / Node v24.18.0 / Raspberry Pi.

Fixes #103684.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added `beforeDeliverTimeoutMs` option (default 30s) to `ReplyDispatcherOptions`.
In `createReplyDispatcher`, each `beforeDeliver` hook is wrapped with a
`Promise.race` deadline — a hung hook returns `null` (cancellation),
`waitForIdle()` resolves, and the lane recovers. Channels with known slow
hooks can configure a longer deadline. Set `0` to disable.

Timer cleanup uses `try/finally` so rejection and fulfillment both clear the
scheduled timer. Timeouts emit a `logWarn` so operators can detect the event.

## User Impact

**Before:** hung channel hook permanently blocks lane, requires restart +
manual `sessions.json` editing
**After:** dispatcher unblocks after timeout, lane recovers automatically.
Timeout is configurable per channel via `beforeDeliverTimeoutMs`.

## Evidence

Branch: `fix/103684-before-deliver-timeout` | Base: `upstream/main`

### Lane recovery proof (simulated WhatsApp scenario from #103684)

```
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof/before-deliver-timeout.mts

=== #103733 lane recovery proof ===

── Scenario: hung beforeDeliver → timeout → lane recovery ──
  Hook hung:        true
  waitForIdle:      true (2057ms)
  Cancelled count:  1 (Real reply)
  Delivered count:  1
  Delivered:        ["Follow-up message after recovery"]

  VERDICT:
    Recovery (waitForIdle < 10s): PASS
    Hung msg cancelled:            PASS
    Next msg delivered:             PASS
    Lane unblocked:                 PASS

  OVERALL: ALL PASSED
```

### Regression tests

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/before-deliver.test.ts

 ✓ cancels delivery before queueing when transformReplyPayload returns null
 ✓ cancels delivery when beforeDeliver returns null
 ... 5 more passing ...

 Test Files  1 passed (1)  Tests  7 passed (7)
```

### Diff summary

```
src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts | 28 ++ (timeout wrapper + option)
scripts/proof/before-deliver-timeout.mts | 65 ++ (lane recovery proof)
```

What was not tested: live WhatsApp channel with real bot credentials. The
proof script exercises `createReplyDispatcher` with the exact `Promise.race`
deadline pattern, proving `waitForIdle()` settles and a subsequent dispatcher
delivers normally — the same sequence a real lane recovery follows.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.

## Linked context

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md

Step 2 — reindex the live agent's memory store:


Step 4 — on the PR branch checkout (`30f15f4e22`), import the modified descriptor/help modules at runtime via `tsx` and print the after-patch strings to prove the new `memory/**/*.md` wording is observable from a real runtime call site (not just the diff):

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
